questions.q: Define Accrued Income and state its treatment in the Balance Sheet.
questions.a: Accrued Income is income earned during the accounting period but not received in cash by the end of the period. It is shown as a **current asset** on the assets side of the Balance Sheet. A wrong answer (e.g., treating it as a liability or ignoring it in the Balance Sheet) reveals the student confuses the *right to receive* (asset) with an *obligation to pay* (liability), or fails to apply the accrual concept that income is recognised when earned, not when received.

questions.q: A business receives ₹50,000 as rent in advance on 1st January 2026 for the period January to December 2026. The accounting year ends on 31st March 2026. Explain how much of this ₹50,000 should be treated as income for the year ended 31st March 2026 and how much as a liability, with reasoning.
questions.a: Only 3 months' rent (January–March) = ₹50,000 × 3/12 = ₹12,500 is income for the current year. The remaining 9 months (April–December) = ₹37,500 is **Unearned Income**, a current liability. A wrong answer (e.g., treating the full ₹50,000 as income or full as liability) reveals the student does not apply the *matching principle* — income must be matched to the period in which it is earned, not when cash is received.

questions.q:
From the following information, pass the adjustment entry and show the treatment in Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet as on 31st March 2026:
"Commission earned but not received ₹8,000."
questions.a:
**Adjustment Entry:**
Commission Accrued A/c Dr. 8,000
   To Commission Received A/c 8,000
(Being commission earned but not received)

**Profit & Loss Account (Credit side):** Add ₹8,000 to Commission Received.
**Balance Sheet (Assets side):** Show ₹8,000 as "Commission Accrued" under Current Assets.
A wrong entry (e.g., debiting Commission Received) or wrong Balance Sheet placement (liability side) reveals the student misunderstands that accrued income *increases* the income earned and creates a *receivable* (asset), not a payable.

questions.q: Compare and contrast Accrued Income and Unearned Income on the basis of: (a) Nature of account, (b) Effect on Profit & Loss Account, (c) Balance Sheet classification, (d) Journal entry direction.
questions.a:
| Basis | Accrued Income | Unearned Income |
|-------|----------------|-----------------|
| (a) Nature | Asset (Receivable) | Liability (Payable) |
| (b) P&L Effect | Added to respective income (increases profit) | Deducted from respective income (decreases profit) |
| (c) B/S Classification | Current Asset | Current Liability |
| (d) Journal Entry | Accrued Income A/c Dr. → Income A/c Cr. | Income A/c Dr. → Unearned Income A/c Cr. |

A wrong comparison reveals the student memorises entries mechanically without understanding the *economic substance*: accrued income = "we did the work, they owe us" (asset); unearned income = "they paid, we owe them work" (liability).

questions.q: A trial balance shows "Interest Received ₹24,000". It is discovered that ₹6,000 of this interest relates to the next accounting period. Evaluate the impact on Net Profit if the accountant fails to adjust for this unearned interest. Justify your answer.
questions.a: Net Profit will be **overstated by ₹6,000**. The ₹24,000 includes ₹6,000 unearned (liability), so only ₹18,000 is current year's income. Without adjustment, the full ₹24,000 is credited to P&L, inflating profit. This violates the *accrual concept* and *matching principle* — income must be recognised in the period it is earned. A wrong answer (e.g., "no impact" or "understated") reveals the student does not grasp that unearned income received in advance *reduces* current period income when adjusted.

questions.q: Create a realistic scenario involving a freelance graphic designer where both Accrued Income and Unearned Income exist simultaneously at year-end. Provide the figures and ask for the adjustment entries, P&L treatment, and B/S presentation.
questions.a:
**Scenario:** As of 31st March 2026, a designer completed a ₹40,000 logo project (client pays in April) and received ₹60,000 advance for a website project starting April 2026 (duration 3 months).
**Adjustment Entries:**
(1) Accrued Income A/c Dr. 40,000 → Fees Earned A/c Cr. 40,000
(2) Fees Earned A/c Dr. 40,000 (60,000 × 2/3 for 2 future months) → Unearned Fees A/c Cr. 40,000
**P&L:** Fees Earned = Original + 40,000 (accrued) – 40,000 (unearned portion)
**B/S:** Accrued Income ₹40,000 (Asset); Unearned Fees ₹40,000 (Liability).
A poor answer (missing one adjustment, wrong proportion for unearned, or wrong B/S sides) reveals the student cannot *simultaneously* apply both concepts in a mixed real-world situation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Accrued Income refers to income that has been earned during the current ______ period but has not yet been received in cash by the end of the period; it is recognised as a current asset.
Fill in the blank: ______ you run a coaching centre and have taught classes in March 2026, but the students pay fees in April 2026.
What is Accrued Income? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Accrued Income refers to income that has been earned during the current accounting period but has not yet been received in cash by the end of the period; it is recognised as a current asset.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Accrued Income?
questions.a: Students often confuse Accrued Income with Unearned Income because both involve a timing difference between cash flow and income recognition.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Pass correct adjustment journal entries for both accrued income and unearned income from a given scenario, (2) Show the treatment of these adjustments in the Profit & Loss Account (credit side for accrued income, deduction from respective income for unearned income) and Balance Sheet (asset for accrued.
